events.label: 4.5 billion years ago
events.title: Giant impact
events.detail: The leading explanation is that a Mars-sized body, Theia, struck the young Earth about 4.5 billion years ago. Debris thrown into orbit gathered into the Moon. Rock ages suggest this happened roughly 60 million years after the solar system began to form.

sources.title: NASA Science: How the Moon formed

events.label: 4.5–4.4 billion years ago
events.title: Magma ocean
events.line: A molten surface, then a crust
events.detail: A magma ocean hundreds to thousands of kilometres deep covered the Moon for tens to hundreds of millions of years. Light anorthosite crystals floated to the top and formed the bright crust; the first crust dates to about 4.4 billion years ago.

sources.title: NASA Science: How the Moon formed

events.label: ~3.9 billion years ago (debated)
events.title: Heavy bombardment
events.detail: Apollo rock ages cluster near 3.9 billion years, which was read as a 'Late Heavy Bombardment', a spike of basin-forming impacts. Boehnke & Harrison (2016) showed argon loss could fake that cluster from a steadily declining impact rate. Chang'e-6 far-side samples also found no clear spike. Whether there was a cataclysm or a slow decline is unresolved.

sources.title: Boehnke & Harrison (2016), Illusory Late Heavy Bombardments, PNAS
Science News: Different moon rocks tell different tales about a long-ago bombardment

events.label: ~4–2 billion years ago
events.title: Dark seas
events.detail: Basalt lava rose from the mantle and flooded huge impact basins, forming the dark maria seen from Earth. Apollo, Luna and Chang'e-5 samples show near-side volcanism between about 4 and 2 billion years ago. Chang'e-6 found far-side basalts about 2.8 billion years old, plus one about 4.2 billion.

sources.title: Li et al. (2024), Lunar farside volcanism 2.8 billion years ago from Chang'e-6 basalts, Nature

events.label: ~800 million years ago
events.title: Copernicus
events.detail: The 93 km Copernicus crater is thought to be about 800 million years old. That age comes from Apollo 12 samples believed to be its ejecta; the link to the crater is inferred.

sources.title: LROC: Copernicus central peak

events.label: ~108 million years ago
events.title: Tycho
events.detail: Tycho, 85 km wide, has bright rays that cross much of the near side. Apollo 17 samples thought to be Tycho ejecta show about 108 million years of exposure, which dates the crater to the age of the dinosaurs.

events.label: 14 September 1959
events.title: Luna 2
events.line: First object to reach the Moon
events.detail: The Soviet Luna 2 probe struck the Moon near Palus Putredinis on 14 September 1959. It was the first human-made object to reach another world.

sources.title: NASA NSSDC: Soviet lunar missions

events.label: 3 February 1966
events.title: Luna 9
events.detail: Luna 9 made the first soft landing on the Moon, in Oceanus Procellarum on 3 February 1966, and sent back the first pictures from the lunar surface.

sources.title: NASA NSSDC: Soviet lunar missions

events.label: 20 July 1969
events.title: Apollo 11
events.detail: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed the lunar module Eagle in Mare Tranquillitatis on 20 July 1969, while Michael Collins orbited above.

sources.title: NASA NSSDC: Apollo landing site coordinates
NASA NSSDC: Apollo missions

events.label: 1970 and 1973
events.title: Lunokhods 1–2
events.detail: Luna 17 landed in Mare Imbrium on 17 November 1970 and released Lunokhod 1, the first rover on another world. Luna 21 delivered Lunokhod 2 to Le Monnier crater on 15 January 1973. Both were driven remotely from Earth.

sources.title: NASA NSSDC: Soviet lunar missions

events.title: Apollo 12–17
events.detail: Apollo 12 (Nov 1969), 14 (Feb 1971), 15 (Jul 1971), 16 (Apr 1972) and 17 (Dec 1972) landed; Apollo 13 aborted. In all, twelve astronauts walked on the Moon and brought back 382 kg of samples. Apollo 17 in December 1972 was the last crewed landing.

events.label: 14 December 2013
events.title: Chang'e 3
events.detail: Chang'e 3 landed in Mare Imbrium on 14 December 2013 with the Yutu rover. It was the first soft landing on the Moon since Luna 24 in 1976.

sources.title: Chang'e 3

events.label: 3 January 2019
events.title: Chang'e 4
events.line: First landing on the far side
events.detail: Chang'e 4 made the first landing on the far side, in Von Kármán crater inside the South Pole–Aitken basin, on 3 January 2019. It relays to Earth through the Queqiao satellite and carried the Yutu-2 rover.

sources.title: Chang'e 4

events.label: 1 December 2020
events.title: Chang'e 5
events.detail: Chang'e 5 landed near Mons Rümker in Oceanus Procellarum on 1 December 2020 and returned about 1.73 kg of soil and rock on 16 December. Its basalts are about 2.0 billion years old, the youngest volcanic rocks dated from the Moon.

sources.title: Chang'e 5

events.label: 23 August 2023
events.title: Chandrayaan-3
events.line: India lands near the south pole
events.detail: ISRO's Vikram lander touched down at about 69.4° S on 23 August 2023. The site was named Shiv Shakti Point, and the landing made India the fourth nation to land softly on the Moon. The Pragyan rover explored nearby.

sources.title: ISRO: Chandrayaan-3

events.label: January–February 2024
events.title: SLIM & Odysseus
events.detail: JAXA's SLIM landed within 100 m of its target near Shioli crater on 19 January 2024, though it ended up on its side. On 22 February 2024 Intuitive Machines' Odysseus (IM-1) became the first commercial lander to touch down softly; it tipped over near Malapert A.

events.label: 1 June 2024
events.title: Chang'e 6
events.detail: Chang'e 6 landed in the Apollo basin on the far side on 1 June 2024 and returned 1,935.3 g of far-side material on 25 June. Its basalts show far-side volcanism about 2.8 billion years ago.

events.label: March 2025
events.title: Blue Ghost
events.detail: Firefly's Blue Ghost Mission 1 landed upright in Mare Crisium on 2 March 2025 and ran its NASA payloads until lunar sunset; it was the first fully successful commercial Moon landing. Four days later Intuitive Machines' Athena (IM-2) reached Mons Mouton near the south pole but tipped over and lost power within a day.

events.label: 1–10 April 2026
events.title: Artemis II
events.detail: On 1 April 2026, SLS launched Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and the Canadian Space Agency's Jeremy Hansen on a nearly 10-day lunar flyby, the first crewed flight beyond Earth orbit since 1972. Orion splashed down off San Diego on 10 April.

events.label: Today
events.title: Today
events.detail: The Moon has no real atmosphere and swings between about −178 °C and 117 °C at the equator. No one has stood on it since 1972. In 2026 NASA reshaped Artemis: Artemis III became an Earth-orbit lander test, the first crewed landing moved to Artemis IV, and Gateway was paused in favour of a south-pole Moon Base. NASA briefed the press on its schedule on 23 October 2026.

events.label: 2027 (planned)
events.title: Robots go south
events.detail: Blue Origin's Blue Moon Mark 1 cargo lander, which slipped out of 2026, is planned for Q1 2027 in NASA's lander timeline, and a later Mark 1 is meant to carry NASA's VIPER rover. China's Chang'e 7, meant to land on the sunlit rim of Shackleton crater to look for ice, missed its August 2026 window; China gave no new date, and press reports say 2027.

events.detail: Artemis III no longer lands. Randy Bresnik, Luca Parmitano (ESA), Frank Rubio and Andre Douglas are to fly Orion into low Earth orbit and dock with test versions of SpaceX's Starship lander and Blue Origin's Blue Moon. NASA says 2027; its HLS timeline says Q3 2027. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman ordered the change in February 2026.

events.label: By end of 2027 (planned)
events.title: Starship lands
events.detail: SpaceX's Starship lander still has to show ship-to-ship propellant transfer in Earth orbit; NASA's timeline puts that test in Q1 2027 and an uncrewed Starship landing by the end of 2027. SpaceX told investors in February 2026 that it was targeting March 2027 for an uncrewed landing (WSJ, via AIAA). Blue Origin's uncrewed Blue Moon Mark 2 landing is planned for Q1 2028.

events.label: 2028 (planned)
events.title: Artemis IV
events.detail: NASA says its first crewed Artemis landing will happen in 2028 on Artemis IV, with Artemis V later in 2028 and then landings about every six months. The lander, Starship or Blue Moon, will be picked after Artemis III. Pins mark the named features of NASA's nine south-pole candidate regions (Oct 2024), not exact landing zones.

events.label: By 2030 (planned)
events.title: China lands crew
events.detail: China's crewed space agency is targeting a crewed landing by 2030. Two Long March 10 rockets would launch the Mengzhou crew ship and the Lanyue lander, which meet in lunar orbit; two astronauts then descend. Abort, landing and rocket tests were done by early 2026.

events.label: 2032 (planned)
events.title: Moon hotel
events.detail: GRU Space, a Y Combinator- and Nvidia-backed startup founded in 2025, plans the first lunar hotel: an inflatable module for up to four guests, delivered by a heavy lander and walled with regolith bricks, then a larger regolith-stone 'grand hotel' shown in its launch film. Roadmap: a subscale inflatable test on a NASA CLPS lander in 2029, a larger mission in 2031, opening in 2032. The grand hotel has no date; here it rises in 2038. All of it depends on landers that are not yet flying.

events.label: By 2035 (planned)
events.title: ILRS basic station
events.detail: China's chief lunar designer Wu Weiren said the basic International Lunar Research Station would be finished by 2035, centred on the south pole; Chang'e 7 and 8 are its first pieces. Russia and China signed a memorandum in May 2025 to build a lunar nuclear power plant for it. Roscosmos has spoken of delivering it in 2033–2035.

events.label: 2026–2036 (planned)
events.title: NASA Moon Base
events.detail: In March 2026 NASA announced a Moon Base near the south pole in three phases. 'Build, Test, Learn' runs through 2028, with robotic landings from 2027. 'Establish Early Infrastructure' (2029–2032) brings habitats, logistics and JAXA's pressurized rover. 'Enable Long-Duration Human Presence' (2033–2036) adds Italy's habitats, Canada's utility vehicle and permanent power systems. The cost is reported at $20 billion over seven years or about $30 billion over a decade.
events.projected_by: NASA (Jared Isaacman, Carlos Garcia-Galan), Ignition event, 24 March 2026

events.label: Within ~10 years (SpaceX, 2026)
events.title: Self-growing city
events.detail: On 8 February 2026 SpaceX CEO Elon Musk wrote that the company had 'already shifted focus to building a self-growing city on the moon', saying 'we can potentially achieve that in less than 10 years, whereas Mars would take 20+ years'. Days later, at an xAI all-hands, he said 'I really want to see a mass driver on the moon that is shooting AI satellites into deep space'. Coverage calls the concept 'Moonbase Alpha'. In January 2025 he had called the Moon 'a distraction'. No site has been named.
events.projected_by: SpaceX — CEO Elon Musk, post on X, 8 February 2026; xAI all-hands, ~11 February 2026
